673.title: Read to the sick
673.hook: ten perceptions read to the sick monk Girimananda, who recovers
673.howItsDone: In parts of the Theravada world, monks chant the Girimananda Sutta for the sick, and visiting and reading to ill people, lay or ordained, is a long-standing Buddhist act of care.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eleven blessings of metta, and your line, wish one person well. Today, a new week, and a different bedside: someone who is ill.

When someone we love is sick, we bring things: soup, flowers, a phone charger, a magazine nobody reads. What we really want to bring is something that helps, and we often don't know what that is. In the Book of Tens, a monk named Girimananda is sick, in pain, gravely ill. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, asks the Buddha to visit him, out of compassion. The Buddha does something unexpected. He doesn't go himself. He sends Ananda back with something to bring: not medicine, but a list of ten things to read aloud.
screen: `WHAT DO WE BRING THE SICK?` → `GIRIMANANDA IS GRAVELY ILL.` → `ANANDA IS SENT WITH A LIST.`

segments.voice: If you tell Girimananda the ten perceptions, the Buddha says, it's possible his illness will subside at once. Then he gives them. One, impermanence: the body, feelings, all of it, changing. Two, not-self: none of it is me or mine. Three, the unattractive: the body seen plainly, hair, skin, bones, the inside as well as the outside. Four, drawbacks: the body as a home for many illnesses, and the text names a long list of them, eye disease to fever. Five, abandoning: letting go of harmful thoughts. Six, dispassion. Seven, cessation. Eight, not delighting in the whole world. Nine, the impermanence of all that's made. Ten, mindfulness of breathing, given in full: breathing in long, breathing out long, and on through sixteen steps. Ananda learns them, goes to Girimananda and recites them, and the text says Girimananda recovered from that illness. It isn't comforting in the usual way. It doesn't say you'll be fine. It looks straight at the body, its fragility and its changes, and ends with the simplest thing a sick person can still do: breathe, and know they're breathing. One modern reading is that a mind steadied and less gripped by fear helps the body. The text itself doesn't explain it; it just says he recovered. In some Theravada communities, this sutta is still chanted for people who are ill.
screen: `THE BUDDHA SENDS ANANDA.` · `IMPERMANENCE, NOT-SELF.` · `ENDING WITH THE BREATH.` · then, large: `HE RECOVERED.`

segments.voice: Settle with the tenth perception: breathing in long, know it; breathing out long, know it. Then bring to mind someone who is unwell, near or far, and picture sitting beside them, wondering what line, message or memory might steady them. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer.

674.title: Inspired, then calm
674.hook: when the mind is scattered, turn to an inspiring theme, then return
674.howItsDone: Some meditation teachers suggest recollecting the Buddha, a teacher or one's own good deeds when practice turns dull or restless, before returning to the main object such as the breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Girimananda's bedside, and your line, ten perceptions. Today, what to do when your own mind won't settle.

Ananda goes one morning to a dwelling of nuns. They sit with him and tell him their practice is going well: we dwell, they say, with our minds well established in the four foundations of mindfulness, and we notice a progress, one stage after another. Ananda is glad, and later he reports it to the Buddha, who agrees: so it is. Then he adds a frank note about how meditation goes. While someone is contemplating, a fever can arise, or sluggishness, or the mind can scatter outward. What then?
screen: `A VISIT TO THE NUNS.` → `IT'S GOING WELL.` → `BUT SOMETIMES...`

segments.voice: Whether you're contemplating the body, or feelings, or mind, or phenomena, the Buddha says, if a fever arises, or sluggishness, or the mind scatters outward, direct the mind toward some inspiring sign, something that lifts the heart. The Pali word, pasadaniya, means something that brings serene confidence. The sutta doesn't say what it is; it might be the Buddha, a teacher, a good deed you remember, a line you love. Then watch the sequence. When the mind turns to the inspiring sign, gladness arises. From gladness, joy. With a joyful mind, the body grows calm. With a calm body, one feels happiness. A happy mind becomes concentrated. Then the second half, the part that's easy to skip. Having been lifted, you withdraw: you set the inspiring image down and return to the original practice. The person then knows, the text says: I'm not thinking and examining; I'm mindful within, and at ease. Not grit your teeth and force it. Not give up and scroll. Lift the heart first, then come back. The Buddha calls this directed development, and he names undirected development too, for when the mind is already steady and doesn't need the detour. The nuns' report was good news, and his answer still makes room for scattered days, with a way back that starts with gladness.

segments.voice: Start with the breath, and if the mind is busy or dull, don't fight it: bring to mind one image that lifts you, a face you admire, a kind act you once saw, a sunrise, the Buddha's still figure, a line you love. Stay with it until a little gladness rises and the body softens. Then set the image down gently and come back to the breath, with a lighter heart.

675.title: Six ways to be dear
675.hook: kindness in deed, word and thought, sharing, virtue and view held together
675.howItsDone: Buddhist monastic communities often teach the six saraniya dhammas as the basis of harmony in the sangha, and lay Buddhist groups sometimes take them as guidelines for family and community life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the nuns, the scattered mind, and your line, look for what lifts you. Today, from one mind to a whole community, and what keeps people close.

Every group that lasts, a family, a team, a congregation, a group chat that's somehow survived ten years, has unspoken reasons it holds together, and every group that falls apart has reasons too. The early monastic community knew both; monks quarreled, and the texts don't hide it. At Kosambi, one sutta says, the monks were stabbing each other with words, and the Buddha taught them this same list. In the Book of Sixes he names six qualities worth remembering, because they create love and respect and lead to harmony, to unity, to not quarreling. The Pali name is saraniya: things to be remembered, or things that make you dear.
screen: `WHY GROUPS HOLD TOGETHER.` → `MONKS QUARRELED TOO.` → `SIX THINGS TO REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: The first three are kindness, in three directions. One: acts of body done with loving-kindness toward your companions, both in public and in private. Two: words spoken with loving-kindness, in public and in private. Three: thoughts held with loving-kindness, in public and in private. That little phrase is the heart of it. Anyone can be kind when watched; what builds trust is the kindness nobody sees. Four: sharing. Whatever you receive, even the contents of your alms bowl, you share with those who keep the same practice, without holding back. For a monk who eats only what he's given, that's his meal. Five: virtue held in common, the same precepts kept unbroken, the kind the wise praise. Six: view held in common, the understanding that leads out of suffering. The order starts with what everyone can do immediately, a kind act, a kind word, and moves toward what grows slowly, a shared way of seeing. And none of the six is about getting others to like you. They're all things you give. Being dear, in this sutta, isn't something you chase. It's what grows around someone who acts, speaks and thinks with kindness, shares, and keeps faith with a common path.
screen: `KIND IN DEED, WORD, THOUGHT.` · `IN PUBLIC AND IN PRIVATE.` · `SHARE EVEN YOUR BOWL.` · then, large: `VIRTUE AND VIEW IN COMMON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a group you belong to, a family, a workplace, a team, a circle of friends, and picture the faces. Think of one thing you could share with them, some food, some time, a skill, good news, credit for a job well done, and picture offering it freely, without keeping score. Then, for a breath or two, wish them all well, quietly, in private.

676.title: Even his back ached
676.hook: the old Buddha warms his back in the sun; Ananda sees his skin loosen
676.tomorrow: A friend gives the hard thing
676.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell this scene when teaching on aging and impermanence, and in Buddhist communities caring for elders, including elderly monks and nuns, is counted as a meritorious act.

segments.voice: Yesterday: saraniya, kindness in public and in private, and the shared bowl. Today, a quiet scene between an old teacher and his attendant.

Evening in Savatthi, at the Eastern Park, in the mansion of Migara's mother. The Buddha has come out of his afternoon seclusion. He's an old man now, sitting in the western sun, warming his back. Ananda, his attendant, comes over and begins to rub his limbs with his hands. It's the kind of moment people who care for an aging parent describe: hands on their arms, and suddenly the skin seems thinner than you remembered. Ananda notices, and he says it out loud.
screen: `AN OLD MAN IN THE SUN.` → `ANANDA RUBS HIS LIMBS.` → `HE NOTICES.`

segments.voice: It's wonderful, sir, it's amazing. Your complexion is no longer clear and bright. Your limbs are slack and wrinkled. Your body is bent forward. And there's a change in your senses: the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body. It's a blunt thing to say to your teacher, and the Buddha doesn't flinch. So it is, Ananda, he says. In youth one is subject to aging; in health, to sickness; in life, to death. Then he speaks a verse that turns on aging itself, scolding it: shame on you, wretched old age, maker of ugliness. Even someone who lives a hundred years, he says, is bound for death; aging spares no one, it crushes everything. And then, the text says, he gets up and goes into town for alms. That last detail is the whole teaching: he names it, scolds it in verse, and goes on with the day. Elsewhere in the canon there are other glimpses, like a day when his back hurts and he asks Sariputta to teach in his place while he lies down to rest it. The texts don't hide the Buddha's body. They show it aging, aching, ordinary. Some readers find that a comfort. Awakening, in this telling, didn't exempt even him from an old man's back.
screen: `YOUR SKIN IS LOOSE, SIR.` · `SO IT IS, ANANDA.` · `A VERSE AGAINST OLD AGE.` · then, large: `THEN HE GOES FOR ALMS.`

segments.voice: If you can, turn your back toward a window or a warm lamp, rest your hands on your forearms, and feel the skin, the warmth, the years in it. Then bring to mind someone older whom you love, and picture warming their back, rubbing their arms, without hurry. Notice what tenderness feels like.
jara. The Pali and Sanskrit word for old age, spoken by the aging Buddha to Ananda in the evening sun: so it is; even life in the body ends in this. Today's word.
Your line: even his. Aging gets named, and the day still goes on, gently. See you tomorrow.

677.title: A friend gives the hard thing
677.hook: seven marks of a friend: gives what is hard to give, does what is hard to do, bears what is hard to bear
677.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers sometimes pair this sutta with the Buddha's teaching on good friendship, kalyanamittata, and lay Buddhists may read it as advice both for choosing friends and for being one.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the old Buddha in the sun, and your line, even his. That scene was also a friendship: Ananda's hands on his teacher's arms. Today, what makes a friend.

Three in the morning, and the phone rings. Who would you call back? Who would call you? Not the people who like your posts; the ones who'd pick up. That list is often short, and it doesn't always match the people we see the most. The Book of Sevens has a short sutta that tries to put that list into words. It's addressed to the monks, but nothing in it is monastic: seven marks of a friend worth keeping close.
screen: `WHO WOULD PICK UP AT 3AM?` → `NOT ALWAYS WHO WE SEE MOST.` → `SEVEN MARKS OF A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: A friend with seven qualities, the Buddha says, is worth associating with. One: they give what is hard to give. Two: they do what is hard to do. Three: they bear what is hard to bear. Four: they tell you their secrets. Five: they keep your secrets. Six: they don't abandon you in misfortune. Seven: they don't look down on you when you're ruined. Look at the first three. Anyone can give what's easy: a like, a quick text, the thing they didn't need anyway. A friend gives what costs something. Their Saturday. Their honesty, when it's awkward. The patience to sit through your bad month. Four and five are a pair: trust going both ways. They let you in, and they don't let your life out. Six and seven: the friend who stays when things fall apart, and who doesn't treat you differently when you've lost. That last one is sharp; it's easy to stay close to someone doing well. The sutta ends in verse, repeating the seven, and says that whoever wants a friend should seek out a person like this. Two days ago, the six ways to be dear described what makes a community hold. This is the same thing at the size of two people, and it can be read both ways at once: a list of friends to look for, and a list of how to be one.
screen: `HARD TO GIVE, DO, BEAR.` · `SECRETS SHARED, SECRETS KEPT.` · `STAYS IN MISFORTUNE.` · then, large: `A FRIEND GIVES THE HARD THING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a friend who once gave you something hard, time, honesty, patience, presence when things were bad, and let yourself feel grateful for a few breaths. Then turn it around: picture a friend who might need something hard from you right now, and which of the seven you could be for them. Rest with that one.

678.title: Pleasure without the hook
678.hook: the monk is taught to eat like a traveler eating to cross the desert
678.howItsDone: Theravada monks and nuns recite a daily reflection on the purpose of food before eating, and many lay Buddhists practice mindful eating, pausing before a meal to consider what it is for.

segments.voice: Yesterday: seven marks of a friend, and your line, give something that costs you. Today, something we do three times a day, and one of the hardest images in the canon.

A fair warning first: today's image is meant to be hard to hear. The early texts sometimes reach for a shocking picture on purpose, so a point can't slide past. Eleven days ago, giving food was life itself. Today, the other side: eating, and the hook that can hide in it. The bag of chips that empties itself. The second dessert nobody wanted. In the Connected Sayings, in a chapter on what the texts call the four kinds of nutriment, the Buddha asks the monks how they should regard their daily food, and answers with a parable about two travelers in a desert.
screen: `A HARD IMAGE, ON PURPOSE.` → `THE HOOK IN EATING.` → `TWO TRAVELERS, A DESERT.`

segments.voice: A husband and wife set out across a desert with a little food, and with their only son, a child they love dearly. Halfway across, the food runs out, and there is no other way to survive. In the parable, they do the unthinkable: weeping, they eat their own child's flesh, to reach the other side. Would they eat that food for fun, the Buddha asks, for pleasure, for decoration, for beauty? No, the monks answer: only to cross the desert. That, he says, is how to regard ordinary food. The image is deliberately unbearable. Nobody could enjoy that meal, and nobody would take one bite more than needed. That's the point. Monks still say a daily reflection, found elsewhere in the canon, that carries the same sense in gentler words: I eat not for fun, not for intoxication, not for looks, but only to keep this body going, to end hunger, and to support the holy life. The teaching isn't that food is bad, or that taste is wrong; lay Buddhists cook beautiful food and offer it with joy. The hook is the extra: eating to fill a mood, to escape, to keep chasing a pleasure that ended three bites ago. So the parable asks a simple question at every meal: what is this for? If the answer is to cross, to live, to be well, the pleasure that comes with it has no hook in it.
screen: `FOOD RUNS OUT IN THE DESERT.` · `THEY EAT ONLY TO CROSS.` · `NOT FOR FUN, NOT FOR LOOKS.` · then, large: `JUST ENOUGH TO CROSS.`

segments.voice: Picture your next meal on the table in front of you, and before you eat, ask the parable's question: what is this for? Let the honest answer come, hunger, energy, comfort, company. Then picture eating slowly, tasting each bite, and noticing the moment you've had enough: not when the plate is empty, but when you've crossed.

ahara. The Pali and Sanskrit word for nutriment or food, behind the parable of the desert travelers in the Connected Sayings: eat as they did, only to cross, and the meal has no hook in it. Today's word.
Your line: just enough to cross. Food isn't the hook; the extra is. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: Does Buddhism say enjoying your food is wrong?

679.title: The pot and the lid
679.hook: like a water pot turned upside down, nothing stays in; an upright pot fills
679.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers sometimes use the three pots when encouraging students to review and practice what they hear, and in some communities Dhamma talks are followed by recitation or discussion to help the teaching stay.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ahara, food, and the desert travelers who ate only to cross. Your line: just enough to cross.

How much of this week stayed with you? Girimananda's bedside. The nuns and the inspiring sign. Six ways to be dear. The old Buddha in the evening sun. Seven marks of a friend. The desert crossing. That's a lot of teaching in seven days. The Book of Threes has a sutta for exactly this question. It sorts listeners into three kinds, with three homely pictures: a pot turned upside down, a lap full of snacks, and a pot standing the right way up.
screen: `HOW MUCH STAYED?` → `A WEEK OF TEACHINGS.` → `THREE KINDS OF LISTENER.`

segments.voice: The first listener goes often to hear the teaching, and it's good in the beginning, middle and end. But they don't attend to any of it, not while sitting, not after they get up. That person, the Buddha says, is like a pot turned upside down. Pour water on it, and it all runs off. The second listener follows while sitting, beginning, middle and end. But once they stand up, it's gone, like a person with sesame seeds and rice cakes in their lap who forgets and stands up, and everything scatters on the ground. The third listener takes it in while sitting and still holds it after getting up: a pot standing upright. Pour water in, and it stays. About today's title: there's no lid in the sutta. There's an upside-down pot, a lap and an upright pot. The lid is my word, and a fair one. Plenty of people listen with a lid on: the phone in one hand, the reply already half-composed. Notice that the first two listeners aren't lazy. They show up and sit through the whole thing. The difference is the angle of the pot. Turning it upright is something you can do: recall a teaching later, repeat it to someone, try it once.
screen: `THE UPSIDE-DOWN POT.` · `THE LAP THAT SPILLS.` · `THE UPRIGHT POT.` · then, large: `KEEP THE POT UPRIGHT.`

segments.voice: Picture a clay pot resting in your lap, mouth up, and let this week's lines pour in, one at a time: ten perceptions; inspired, then calm; six ways to be dear; even his; a friend gives the hard thing; just enough to cross. Notice which ones stayed in and which ran off, with no grading. Then hold the one that matters most to you for a few breaths.
avakujja. The Pali word for upside down, naming the first of three listeners in the Book of Threes: an upside-down pot, a spilling lap, and an upright pot that holds what's poured in. Today's word.
Your line: keep the pot upright. What's poured in can stay. Day six hundred seventy-nine, done.

chat.says: You went to that talk. Does it matter if you forget it all afterward?
options: Yes: hearing it isn't the same as holding it, like an upright pot.
No: the sutta says forgetting is fine as long as you showed up.
